# Appeal of Denial — Hip Arthroscopy (CPT 29914)

**Governing Policy:** Aetna CPB 0736 – Hip Preservation Surgery (https://www.aetna.com/cpb/medical/data/700_799/0736.html), last review 07/31/2026

**RE:** Appeal of Adverse Benefit Determination dated 2026-08-24
**Member:** Taylor Foster
**Member ID:** W492196775
**Reference Number:** POC-C65CA65DA3-33163
**Plan:** Aetna (Commercial/ACA), Wyoming
**Requested Service:** Hip arthroscopy, CPT 29914

Dear Aetna Appeals Review Team,

I am appealing the denial of my hip arthroscopy (CPT 29914), which Aetna denied on 2026-08-24 on the grounds that my records do not document an adequate trial of conservative treatment before surgery. My surgeon, Dr. Okafor, has documented that this procedure is medically necessary, and I am asking Aetna to reconsider this decision based on my treatment history and the plan's own policy.

**What my records show about conservative treatment**

Before requesting surgery, I completed the following non-surgical treatment for my hip condition:

- **24 months** of progressive hip pain, unrelieved by rest.
- **14 weeks of supervised physical therapy** (18 visits) focused on core and hip stabilization with activity modification, from 2026-04-27 to 2026-08-03, as documented in the physical therapy discharge note.
- **8 months of NSAID use** with inadequate relief.
- A **corticosteroid injection on 2026-06-14**, which gave only 4 weeks of partial relief.
- An **MRI arthrogram on 2026-07-11** confirming an anterosuperior labral tear with cam-type femoroacetabular impingement (alpha angle 68 degrees), with joint space preserved and Tonnis grade 0.
- Ongoing sharp anterior groin pain with sitting and pivoting, inability to run or squat, and positive provocative testing on exam.

**How this compares to the plan's own criteria**

I want to be transparent about what I am and am not able to quote here. The policy language provided to me for this appeal is drawn from Aetna CPB 0736's criteria for pelvic osteotomy (PAO), iliopsoas tenotomy following hip replacement, and gluteus medius tendon repair. The policy states:

> "Minimum 6 months of symptoms;"

This specific line appears in the section governing pelvic osteotomy for acetabular dysplasia, which is not my diagnosis or my requested procedure. I am not asking Aetna to treat this as the literal standard for hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement. I raise it only to note that, even under this related standard elsewhere in the same policy, Aetna's own benchmark for how long symptoms must be present before surgery is considered is far shorter than the 24 months documented in my records.

The policy also states:

> "Arthroscopic surgery in concert with an osteotomy would be assessed using the medical necessity criteria noted above for arthroscopic surgery of the hip."

This tells me that CPB 0736 contains a specific section of criteria for arthroscopic surgery of the hip, separate from the PAO criteria quoted above. That section was not included in the material available to me, and it was also not quoted in the denial notice I received. I am respectfully asking Aetna to identify and apply the specific arthroscopy criteria from CPB 0736 to my case, and to explain in writing which specific element of that criteria my conservative-care record is said to fail, since the denial notice did not specify this.

The policy states that its criteria exist to "further define those indications for services that are proven safe and effective" and are "based upon evidence-based guidelines and clinical studies in the peer-reviewed published medical literature." I believe my treatment history — 14 weeks of supervised physical therapy, 8 months of NSAID therapy, and a corticosteroid injection, all without lasting relief, alongside MRI-confirmed structural pathology — reflects a substantial and reasonable trial of conservative care consistent with that evidence-based intent.

**What I am asking**

I am requesting that Aetna reconsider this denial in light of:
1. The extensive conservative treatment documented above, and
2. The specific arthroscopy criteria in CPB 0736 referenced in the policy but not yet identified to me or applied to my case.

If Aetna's arthroscopy-specific criteria require something different from what is in my records, I ask that this be stated clearly so my surgeon and I can respond directly to it.

**Deadline and submission**

I understand this appeal must be received by **2027-02-20** (180 days from the denial notice, per Aetna's policy, though the denial letter is authoritative). I am submitting this appeal using Aetna's Member Complaint and Appeal Form, available through my account at aetna.com under complaints, grievances and appeals, and/or by fax to 859-425-3379. I will confirm the correct appeal address printed on my denial letter before sending.

Please let me know if any additional information is needed from me or from Dr. Okafor's office to complete this review.

Sincerely,

[Signature]
Taylor Foster
Member ID: W492196775
[Phone number]
[Email address]
[Date]

---

*This letter is not medical or legal advice and does not guarantee that coverage will be approved.*

quotes: Aetna considers pelvic osteotomy (e.g., peri-acetabular osteotomy (PAO)) medically necessary for a diagnosis of acetabular dysplasia (not borderline dysplasia) for persons who fulfill all of the following criteria:
Aetna considers pelvic osteotomy in skeletally immature children medically necessary for a diagnosis of acetabular dysplasia.
Medically Necessary Procedures Medically necessary procedures, when above criteria are met, include:

Endoscopic tenotomy (or lengthening) for iliopsoas tendinopathy following total hip arthroplasty with the failure of at least 6 weeks of formal in-person physical therapy in the past year, and at least 1 therapeutic injection (steroid with or without local anesthetic) with significant but temporary benefit in the past 6 months.
Repair of complete gluteus medius tears is considered medically necessary.
for members with moderate or worse arthritis (Tonnis 2 or 3), the procedure would be considered not medically necessary;
Arthroscopic surgery in concert with an osteotomy would be assessed using the medical necessity criteria noted above for arthroscopic surgery of the hip.

The supplemental medical necessity criteria in this CPB further define those indications for services that are proven safe and effective where those indications are not fully established in applicable NCDs and LCDs.
These supplemental medical necessity criteria are based upon evidence-based guidelines and clinical studies in the peer-reviewed published medical literature.

The background section of this CPB includes an explanation of the rationale that supports adoption of the medical necessity criteria and a summary of evidence that was considered during the development of the CPB;

While there is a possible risk of reduced or delayed care with any coverage criteria, Aetna believes that the benefits of these criteria – ensuring patients receive services that are appropriate, safe, and effective – substantially outweigh any clinical harms.
